results.title: US automotive tariffs drive uncertainty across supply chains
results.content:
On 3 May, the US imposed a 25% tariff on all imported auto parts, completing a two-stage package that already targeted finished vehicles. While those with at least 85% North American content are exempt, most cross-border supply chains face upheaval.

With warnings that the new duties could increase car prices by US$2,000 to US$12,000, consumer confidence dropped for a fifth straight month in April, hitting 86.0—its lowest level since COVID-19. [...] Deeds predicts a potential rush into Foreign-Trade Zones (FTZs), the bonded sites where duties can be deferred or, for parts assembled into finished vehicles, reduced. Regulators are weighing a flat 25% rate on parts and cars, threatening to nullify the usual FTZ savings. This could lead to court challenges and uncertainty. “We could get a red-light, green-light situation. Yes, the tariffs are on, no, they’re off, until the judges decide months from now,” she warned. results.title: Tariff Resources and Strategies | GaMEP at Georgia Tech
results.content:
As global trade evolves, manufacturers — either directly or indirectly — may face new challenges, such as adjusting pricing strategies, disrupting supply chains, and rising production expenses.

However, you can manage your risk and reduce your tariff burden through expert guidance and strategic solutions:

## Alternative Tariff Strategies [...] ## GaMEP Expertise

 Supply chain assessment: We evaluate your supply chain — from raw material to finished product — to identify risks and opportunities.
 Supplier scouting: We search for and connect you with qualified domestic suppliers.

 Process improvement: We apply lean practices to improve production and reduce costs.
 Technology automation: We analyze and help implement appropriate technologies. [...] Reshoring: Consider automation opportunities and domestic suppliers (including those who can expand their production).
 Nearshoring: Take advantage of duty-free imports through Mexico.
 Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States Chapter 98 and Chapter 99: Eliminate or reduce duties for qualifying products.
 Bonded warehouses: Store imported products while deferring duties until they leave the facility (quarterly harbor maintenance fees apply).

results.title: Chain Reaction: US Tariffs and Global Supply Chains
results.content: Tariff uncertainty: Manufacturing firms today face mixed messages on US trade goals and high uncertainty about long-term tariff levels. Maximizing tariff revenues requires the US to have low enough tariffs to preserve import volumes, but incentivizing onshoring to the US requires very high tariffs in strategic sectors. Inflation management and China de-risking are additional considerations. In short, until US goals are clarified, firms will find it hard to plan around future tariff levels. [...] of imported cars. Mexico, too, is raising tariffs on Chinese content (at the urging of the US but also for its own trade defense purposes), raising the prospects of a USMCA renegotiation that preserves regional integration and deepens the formation of shared barriers to Chinese exports. [...] Supply chains tend to move when goods can be manufactured in countries with lower “landed costs”—the cost of production plus shipping, customs duties, and insurance. Tariffs directly impact these calculations, which helps explain why US imports from China declined after the US imposed Section 301 tariffs on $550 billion of imports from China in 2017 (Figure 1).
